 View Comments The Iowa Capitol building. Charlie Neibergall/AP Photo/Charlie Neibergall The Iowa chapter of the Salem-based Satanic Temple has prevailed in its legal fight to participate in a holiday event in the Capitol rotunda in Des Moines after having its application denied three years in a row by Republican state officials, federal court records show. 
 The organization has similarly tangled with leaders in Boston, New Hampshire , and elsewhere. 
 A federal judge on Monday gave the Iowa Department of Administrative Services seven days to approve the Satanic Temple Iowa’s application to take part in a one-day public holiday event scheduled for Dec. 12, saying the organization had shown “a likelihood of success on its free speech claim.” 
 The Satanic Temple on Bridge Street in Salem. Katherine McCabe/Globe Photo Mark Campbell, director of the department and a named defendant, immediately filed a notice indicating his office’s intention to appeal US Chief District Judge Stephanie M. Rose’s order. 
 Satanic Temple Iowa sued the state in August, alleging discrimination and violation of free speech and freedom of expression. The organization’s complaint said its applications for the holiday event in 2024 and 2025 were denied and its 2026 application had been pending for 159 days without a decision. 
 Iowa state officials denied the organization’s 2026 application in September after the lawsuit was filed in federal court in Des Moines. 
 The temple was founded in 2013 in Salem . It says it does not believe in Satan but is a “non-theistic religious organization. It bills itself as “the primary religious Satanic organization in the world” that works to “preserve and advance secularism and individual liberties.” 
 Iowa state officials argued that the organization’s display would include costumery that could be harmful to minors and the capitol’s building policies prohibit gratuitous violence and obscene displays. 
 An evidentiary hearing was held in Des Moines on Oct. 6. Campbell was among four witnesses to testify, court records show. 
 Of particular concern to state officials was imagery of Krampus, a horned, European folkloric character, said to accompany Saint Nicholas during the Christmas season to punish misbehaving children. 
 Campbell testified that he did no independent research about Krampus but heard about the character as a child. 
 “What the Department may not do is exclude the event because Director Campbell understands Krampus to be a figure who harms children and takes them to hell,” Rose wrote in her 24-page order. 
 Rose added that additional concern about sticks carried as part of the group’s costumes “cannot justify denying the entire event.” 
 The American Civil Liberties Union of Iowa represented the Satanic Temple. 
 “Too often, fear or misunderstanding of the ‘other’ is amplified by petty governmental bureaucrats looking to score cheap political points by portraying unfamiliar beliefs as ‘dangerous,’” Matt Kezhaya, the temple’s attorney, said in a statement. 
 “This was always going to be a family-friendly event,” he said. “None of this became ‘harmful’ just because state officials disapproved of our chosen expression.” 
 In New Hampshire, city officials in Concord in 2024 opted to allow the temple to feature a holiday display in front of the New Hampshire State House to avoid litigation. 
 In 2024, The Satanic Temple in New Hampshire and Vermont secured a permit for a Baphomet display, ahead of the Sol Invictus holiday on Dec. 25 at a city plaza in front of the New Hampshire State House in Concord. Amanda Gokee/Globe Staff In 2021, the temple sued Boston, claiming the council was guilty of religious discrimination for refusing to let a representative from the group give an invocation before a meeting. The temple lost its federal appeal alleging religious discrimination. 
 Material from the Associated Press was used in this report.
